# The Peculiar Joy of Autumn Leaves

I've been thinking about leaves lately—specifically, how we've collectively decided that trees dying is beautiful.

It's genuinely strange when you consider it. A leaf turns red and gold not as a triumphant flourish but because it's literally shutting down. The brilliant colors emerge only after the chlorophyll drains away. We're watching decomposition, and we've made it our favorite season.

Yet somehow this makes perfect sense.

There's something honest about autumn that spring, for all its promise, can't quite manage. Spring is all potential energy—the world saying "what if?" Autumn is acceptance. Here's what we've created this year. Here's what we're letting go. The brightness isn't denial of what's coming; it's defiance because of it.

I think we need that defiance more than we admit. We live in a culture obsessed with permanence—keeping things new, young, unchanging. We fight seasons in ourselves the way we fight them in nature, spending billions to resist what's inevitable. So when October arrives, maybe we're not really celebrating the leaves.

Maybe we're celebrating permission.

Permission to change dramatically. Permission for things to end beautifully. Permission to acknowledge that the most stunning moments often contain loss, and that's not tragic—it's just real, and reality can be gorgeous when you stop fighting it.

The leaves don't apologize for falling. They just burn brightly on the way down.
